opener.heading: Week 40: Numbers & Counting 🔢
about: Azlyn can recite numbers to twenty and still not know what one of them means. Every number this week lands on something she can touch, hear or stand on. Friday she builds a board game and numbers twenty squares in her own hand. Saturday she lays eight places for eight guests and finds the one that is short a spoon. Sunday the numbers arrive as coins dropping into a cookie tin with her eyes shut. Monday she runs a hall floor taped 0 to 10, Tuesday she climbs eight stairs with her voice rising a note a step, Wednesday she runs that same hall and stops dead on the number she picked herself, and by Thursday she reads four dots off a card and plays them back on a bucket.

No holiday lands this week, so October does the work: one tree with half its leaves up and half already down, sidewalk she can kick through, wet railings that ring under a stick, and the light going gold by five. Two threads run the week. On five of the seven days the counting jar comes down for one round at a time and goes back on a high shelf after, because everything in it is the size that chokes Kreston. The hall number line goes down on Monday and stays taped until Thursday afternoon, when she walks it one last time and peels it up.
azlyn: One number for one thing. Forty objects into a jar, eight plates onto a table, a finger on each as she goes. Touching every item is what stops the count drifting.
The numerals 0 to 10. She writes them on cards, tapes them down the hall, and runs to the one you call without counting up from the start.
Counting sounds she cannot see. Coins into a tin behind a dish towel, knocks through a closed door, four beats on a pan. The number has to be held in her head.
Stopping on a number. A tower that halts at seven with the next cup already in her hand, and a run down the hall that ends where the count says it ends.
Rules she invents and then has to live with. She dictates the board game rules onto a card, and they bind her the same as they bind you.
you: Inventing a game is a much bigger deal than playing one
Hosting is a social skill, and it's learnable at three
Predicting a sound and then testing it is her first real hypothesis
Loud is a developmental need, not a provocation
High and low is a confusing pair of words
Freezing on cue is genuine impulse control
Copying a rhythm is harder than it looks, and it's a working memory task
shopping: A large jar or clear tub with a lid, for the counting jar
Forty small objects: buttons, coins, dried pasta, bottle caps
A large cardboard box, the biggest in the house, to flatten
A shoebox with a lid, or a cereal box
A cereal box to cut six cards from
Blank cards, 11, cut from card or another box
Plain paper, a stack of letter-size sheets
Paper cups, 2, one of them the bean shaker
Napkins, or 8 squares of paper towels
Cushions, 5 (four for the guests, one for Kreston well back from the buckets)
Crackers, a banana, and grapes to quarter lengthways
Cookies and fruit to cut, for the tea party
A small pitcher she can lift with two hands, and water or juice for it
Buckets, tins and saucepans in 5 different sizes
A sock ball or a beanbag
Jam jars or glass tumblers, 8, all the same size
Food coloring, one drop a jar, optional
Blocks or small boxes for Kreston, 4
Music on your phone, in case the pan is too much on Wednesday
A stair gate that shuts, for Tuesday afternoon
Potatoes and peas for dinner, for her counting jobs
opener.krestonNote: Kreston is 15 months this week. He runs, spoons his own food and points at pictures in books, so name whatever his finger lands on and then say how many of them there are. He turns 16 months on Tuesday the 5th, and from that morning he stacks four blocks, copies whatever chore you are doing, and has ten words or more to work with.

days.title: Her Own Board Game
days.prepTonight: Flatten the biggest box in the house and stand it behind the sofa, and put out a jar and forty small things for the morning.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: Forty Things in the Counting Jar

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: How Many Steps to the Mailbox

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Board and the Card Counters

opening.title: Forty Things in the Counting Jar
opening.need: 1 large jar or clear tub with a lid · 40 small objects (buttons, coins, dried pasta, bottle caps) · 1 tray.
steps: Tip the forty objects onto the tray and push it in front of her. She sorts before she counts, so let that run.
Count ten into your hand out loud, one object per number, and drop them in the jar. She loads the other thirty.
Ask how many are in there. Take her answer as it comes and tell her the jar is the bank for the game she builds at 9:15.

main.title: The Track With Twenty Squares
materials: 1 straight strip of card to rule the lines
3 dried butter beans, one side of each colored with the marker
Paper and a pencil for her rules
steps: Lay the flattened box on the floor. Rule a snaking track of twenty squares across it with the marker and the card strip, each square wide enough for her hand.
Hand her the marker. She numbers the squares 1 to 20 herself. Backwards fives and a 12 running off the edge all count. Write the numerals she asks for.
Color one side of each butter bean. Drop all three in the paper cup, shake, tip them out and count the colored sides facing up. That is how many squares you move.
She picks the counters out of the jar, a button for her and a bottle cap for you. Tape a strip across square one, write START on it, and tape another across twenty.

Play one round with no rules. Somewhere in it she will announce one. Write every rule she invents on the paper with the pencil, word for word, then read the list back before the next game and play by all of it.
main.tip: Her rules will favor her. Play them straight and lose. She is watching to see whether a rule she made holds when it costs you the game.

outside.title: How Many Steps to the Mailbox
paras: Walk to the mailbox counting your steps out loud, one number per foot, and let her count hers coming back. Count curbs and drain covers on the way home.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, so let him walk the last stretch on his own feet with one hand in yours. Count his steps out loud too, slow, one number per step.

second.title: The Game in a Box
second.intro: Getting the game to the grandparents at half past two means packing it into something she can carry.
materials: 1 shoebox or cereal box with a lid
Thick card for the counters and the rules card
The board, the paper cup, the beans and the jar counters from this morning
steps: Count the players out loud, teddies included. Cut one counter from thick card for each of them while she calls out the shapes she wants.
She colors every counter and draws a face on it. Write the name of its owner on the back in marker.
Swap the card counters onto the board, tip the buttons and bottle caps back into the jar, and put the jar up on a high shelf.
Fold the board in half, press the crease flat and run masking tape along it so it folds without tearing.
She dictates the rules and you write them on the card in marker, one per line, with a small picture beside each so she can read them back on her own.
Load the box: counters, cup, beans, rules card. The folded board goes in the paper bag with the box on top, and she writes the name of the game on the lid in crayon.
Play one game out of the packed box before it goes anywhere.
second.tip: Let her carry the bag herself. A game she made and hauled to another house is worth more than one she was handed.

alternatives: Counters and the shaker cup only, no rules card.
Draw a five-square track instead and play it twenty times.
Count out forty objects into groups of ten on the rug.
Tape twenty numbered squares on the hall floor and walk them.
outAgain: The grandparents, and she runs the game with her rules card in her hand
A friend's house, if the grandparents are out
The park, where the light goes gold early now
A walk to the mailbox, counting gates on the way there and back

aroundWorld.title: Counting on Your Hands, Everywhere 🖐️
paras: Hands count higher than ten across a lot of the world. In parts of India, Pakistan and Egypt people count the joints of the four fingers with the thumb, which reaches twelve on one hand. Chinese hand numbers run to ten on a single hand, a different finger shape for each.
aroundWorld.tryIt: Count twelve raisins onto her plate the Indian way, thumb walking up the finger joints, three joints to a finger.
aroundWorld.didYouKnow: Counting finger joints is where the dozen comes from. Twelve eggs in a box, twelve months in a year.

days.krestonPM: Give him the shoebox lid and four card offcuts at the grandparents' feet. At 15 months he fills a container and empties it again for as long as anyone keeps handing the pieces back.

insight.headline: Inventing a game is a much bigger deal than playing one.
paras: Playing a game means holding somebody else's rules in your head. Making one means deciding what the rules are, which needs her to imagine a system that does not exist yet and then hold it steady while other people act inside it. Three-year-olds who invent games run ahead on planning and on the flexible thinking that lets them change a rule once it stops working. Her rules will be unfair and they will drift mid-game, and she will hold you to them harder than she holds herself. Write them down anyway and play by them. Treating her system as real is what keeps her building systems.

days.safety: The counting jar holds buttons, coins, dried pasta and bottle tops, every one of them the size that chokes a 15-month-old who runs and still puts things in his mouth. The jar goes up high the moment counting stops, and it stays up all week. The scissors stay with you. Counting drain covers puts both of them at the curb, so hold his hand from the curb onward, keep the grating on your side of him, and walk Azlyn on the house side.

days.title: Eight Places at the Table
days.prepTonight: Clear the table and stack eight plates, eight cups and eight spoons on the side, and quarter the grapes lengthways before you go up.

opening.title: A Chair for Every Guest
steps: Tell her eight are coming to a party at her table today and ask who they are. Take the list as she gives it, teddies and all.
Count the guests with her, one finger per name, and stop at eight however you get there.

Set four chairs at the table and lay four cushions along the far edge of the table, so the smaller guests sit up at it. Count the eight seats out loud, then count the eight guests again, and leave the table bare.

main.title: Setting Eight Places
materials: 8 napkins or squares of paper towels
Paper and 1 marker for the numbered place cards
The snack to divide: crackers, grapes quartered lengthways, sliced banana
steps: Fold eight bits of paper into standing cards and write 1 to 8 on them in marker while she watches. She adds her own marks to each one.
She walks the table and puts one card at each place. Eight cards, eight guests, and she will land on seven or nine the first time.
Load the tray with eight plates. She carries and lays them one per card, then comes back for the cups, the spoons and the napkins, one kind of thing per trip.
Take one spoon away while she is looking elsewhere. Walk round the table touching each place and counting out loud, and let her find the place that is short.
Sit the guests down. Chairs for the four who need them, cushions for the four who do not.
Snack at 10:15 happens at her table. One cracker, one slice of banana and two grape quarters on every plate, counted out by her.
main.tip: She will lose count at six and start from one again. Let her, as often as she needs.

outside.title: Eight Leaves for Eight Places
paras: Take a paper bag out and bring back eight leaves, one for every place at the table. Early October is the best week of the year for it: yellow, green, brown and red on one tree. Count them into the bag and out again on the doorstep.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and spoons his own food, so give him a real place at the table with a plate and a spoon rather than a tray on the floor. His come out of the cupboard and sit outside her count, because the eight are hers. Outside, let him carry one leaf the whole way home in his fist.

second.title: The Tea Party She Runs
second.intro: Eight places are laid and nothing has happened at them yet. She hosts.
materials: 1 small pitcher of water or juice she can lift with two hands
A plate of cookies and cut fruit
1 notepad and 1 pencil for the orders
The counting jar as the register
steps: She stands at the door and lets the guests in one at a time, showing each to a numbered place. You carry the teddies and wait to be seated.
She goes round with the notepad and the pencil and takes everyone's order. Her writing is a scribble per guest.
Two of everything onto each plate off the serving plate, cookies and fruit, counted out loud as she goes.
Pouring. Both hands on the pitcher, one cup at a time, and the dish towel is hers for what lands on the table.
Set the counting jar beside her as the register. Everyone pays at the end and she counts out what she is owed, one button per guest.
Goodbyes at the door, one guest at a time, counted out of the room as they leave. Eight in, eight out.
Clear together. She stacks the cups in fours and tells you how many that makes.
second.tip: Order something awkward. Ask for four cookies and no fruit and let her say no.

alternatives: Four places instead of eight, and a party for two.
A picnic on the floor with the same eight plates.
Wash up the whole party at the sink in warm water.
Draw the table from above and put eight circles on it.
outAgain: The museum, first Saturday of October and the tenth of the year
The library, if the museum is booked out
The park and the leaf pile, if nobody can face a building today
The thrift store, hunting a teapot for the next party
days.krestonPM: Carry him for the first room at the museum and put him down in the second. At 15 months he points at pictures, so watch where his finger goes and name whatever it lands on.

insight.headline: Hosting is a social skill, and it's learnable at three.
paras: Greeting somebody, seating them, asking what they want and handing it over in the right order is a long chain of steps held together by attention to another person. Azlyn has spent three years on the receiving end of it, and running the party herself flips her into the role that has to track what everyone else needs. That tracking is perspective-taking, the thing that makes sharing and turn-taking possible later. She will forget a guest and pour for herself first. The sequence is what she is learning, and she gets it from doing the job rather than from being reminded to be polite.

days.safety: Party food ends up on the floor and Kreston is down there at speed. Grapes quartered lengthways, no whole nuts, nothing hot within reach of either child, and a sweep between the party and the crawling. The counting jar goes back up high the moment the register closes.

days.title: Counting With Her Ears
days.prepTonight: Empty a metal cookie tin and stand it on the table with ten coins or smooth pebbles beside it, and put the counting jar within your reach and not hers.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: One at a Time Into the Tin

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Knock Three Times, Bring Me Three

schedule.label: Quiet Play
schedule.name: The Tin and the Dish Towel

opening.title: One at a Time Into the Tin
opening.need: 1 empty metal cookie tin · 10 coins or smooth pebbles.
steps: Drop one coin into the empty tin from a hand's height. Then two, one after the other, a beat apart, and say the number each time it lands.
Hand her the coins. She drops, you count out loud, and the two of you find the speed where the numbers still fit between the sounds.
Tip the tin out and count them back in together. Tell her that at 9:15 she does the same job with her eyes shut.

main.title: How Many Did You Hear
materials: 1 dish towel to hide the drops
steps: Sit facing each other across the table with the tin between you and the dish towel draped over your dropping hand.
She shuts her eyes. Drop between one and five coins, one at a time with a clear gap, and let her say the number before she opens them.
Count them out of the tin together to check. She will be right on two and three long before she is right on five.
Swap over. She drops, you guess, and you get one wrong on purpose to see what she does with that.
Change the sound. Dried pasta lands soft, a pebble lands hard, and the wooden spoon on the tin rim is louder than either. Ask her which is easiest to count and take her answer.
Refill from the counting jar when the coins run short, and put the jar back up high when you finish.
main.tip: Leave a full second between drops. Two sounds that arrive together are one sound to her, and the gap is what turns a noise into a number.

outside.title: One Finger for Every Sound
paras: Walk to a bench, sit down and shut your eyes for a slow count of ten. One finger goes up for every separate sound: a car, a dog, a plane, feet on wet leaves. Compare hands at the end. October Sunday mornings are quiet enough for this to work and cold enough that you both want to move again after.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and points at whatever he notices. Sit him on the bench between you and watch where his finger goes when a plane crosses over. Name it, then say how many, and he gets the count attached to the thing he already found.

second.title: Knock Three Times, Bring Me Three
second.intro: A number she cannot see has to be held in her head long enough to act on it. The knocking is the order and the basket is the answer.
materials: A door or the table to knock on
Paper and 1 crayon for the tally
steps: Knock three times on the table, slow. She fetches three things from the room and puts them in the basket, whatever they turn out to be.
Count them out together. Draw three marks on the paper with the crayon and write 3 at the end of the row.
Go up and down between one and five. Empty the basket after each round so she starts from nothing.
Move out of sight and knock on the door instead. She has to count with nothing to look at, which is the version she finds hard.
Swap over. She knocks with the wooden spoon and sends you off, and you come back with the wrong number twice so she gets to correct you.
Counting jar round: she counts that many buttons out of the jar into the basket, then tips them back and the jar goes up high.
Finish on a big one. Knock eight times and watch her carry what she can and come back for the rest.
second.tip: She will start moving before you have finished knocking. Say the count out loud with the last few knocks for a round or two, then drop your voice again.

alternatives: Clap the number instead of knocking.
Hide five things around the room and send her after them one at a time.
Fill the basket with the same five things over and over.
Bang the tin from the next room and count through the wall.
outAgain: A playground you have never been to, and count the swings before she gets on one
The duck pond, counting ducks in and ducks out
A long Sunday walk with the stroller, counting bridges and gates
The woods, kicking through whatever came down in the wind this week
A drive somewhere with a hill and a view
days.krestonPM: Take the basket out with you. At 15 months he carries a thing while he runs and hands it over when somebody puts a hand out, so let him load one leaf at a time into the basket at the playground. Buckeyes stay in your pocket. Count the leaves onto the doorstep with him when you get home.

insight.headline: Predicting a sound and then testing it is her first real hypothesis.
paras: Azlyn hears four drops, says four, opens her eyes and counts four coins in the tin. She has made a claim, checked it against the world and found out she was right, which is the shape of every experiment she will ever run. Guessing from sound alone forces her to hold a count in her head without the steadying help of fingers or objects, and that mental version arrives later than the pointing kind. Being wrong matters as much as being right here. The tin hands her the answer without anybody having to tell her, and a wrong guess sends her straight back in for another round.

days.safety: Coins, pebbles, dried pasta and buttons are every one of them the size that chokes a 15-month-old, and Kreston runs. Sweep the floor between rounds, count the coins back into the tin before he goes down, and the counting jar goes up high the moment the round ends.

days.title: Loud Numbers
days.prepTonight: Stand five buckets, tins or saucepans of different sizes in the middle of the living room floor with two wooden spoons across the top of them.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Zero to Ten Down the Hallway

opening.title: Five Buckets, Biggest to Smallest
opening.need: 5 buckets, tins or saucepans in different sizes · 1 wooden spoon.
steps: Line the five up across the floor, biggest to smallest, and let her move any she disagrees with.
Tap each one twice with the spoon, working down the line. The big ones boom and the small ones ring, and she will hear the order change.
Ask her which one is the loudest and let her prove it. That one goes on the end and it is number five at 9:15.

main.title: Five Is the Loudest
materials: 5 buckets, tins or saucepans in different sizes
1 sheet of card folded into a 1-to-5 dial
steps: Put Kreston on his cushion at the far end of the room, a good distance back, before anything gets hit.
Stick a strip of masking tape on each bucket and number them 1 to 5 in marker, quietest to loudest, in the order she settled on at breakfast.
Fold the card into five panels and write a big numeral on each. That is the dial, and she holds it.
She shows a number and everyone plays eight beats at that volume. Count the eight out loud together, spoons on the buckets, and stop dead on eight.
She changes the number between rounds. One is a fingertip on the rim, five is both spoons on the big bucket, and she calls which arrives.
Count down to finish. Five, four, three, two, one, then zero, and zero is silence held for a slow count of five with the spoons on the floor.
main.tip: Give her the dial and keep your hands on a bucket. A three-year-old told all week to keep it down plays the quiet numbers with care once the loud ones are hers to call.

outside.title: Loud Twenty, Quiet Twenty
paras: Find a path with nobody's window on it and count twenty steps at the top of your voices, then twenty more in a whisper. October wind takes the loud numbers off across the field, and the quiet ones make her lean in to hear yours.

days.infant: Kreston is 15 months and runs, so let him do the loud twenty on his own feet between you. Watch his face on the quiet twenty: dropping to a whisper makes most 15-month-olds copy the volume before they copy the words.

second.title: Zero to Ten Down the Hallway
second.intro: The hall floor becomes a number line this afternoon, and it stays down until Thursday.
materials: A clear stretch of hall floor
steps: Write 0 to 10 on the eleven sheets in marker, one numeral per sheet, and let her do the ones she can.
Tape them down the hall, a stride apart, 0 at the near end and 10 at the far one. She lays them, you tape.
Walk the line together saying each number as a foot lands on it. Then back the other way, 10 down to 0.
Call a number and she runs to it. Call another before she has stopped. Six or seven rounds and she stops looking at 0 to work out where 7 is.
Throw the sock ball down the line. She fetches it, names the number it landed on and counts her steps back to you.
Stand her on 3 and ask for two steps forward. Ask where she is now.
Leave the whole thing taped down. She will walk it on her own at 4:15 and you need it again on Wednesday and Thursday.

alternatives: Line up to five only, and jump it.
Chalk the same line outside if the hall is impossible.
Lay the numbers out of order and let her sort them.
Hop it on one foot, then walk it backwards.
outAgain: The hill walk, counting the stops on the way up
The neighborhood park, and the long way round
A field walk in rain boots, because the ground has turned
The playground with the big slide
days.krestonPM: He will be on the number line the second it is down. At 15 months he walks a taped path for the pleasure of the line under his feet, and the numbers mean nothing to him yet. Say them anyway as he passes each sheet. Tape the corners flat so nobody skids on a loose one.

insight.headline: Loud is a developmental need, not a provocation.
paras: Banging a saucepan is how Azlyn finds out what her arms can do to the world. She is calibrating force against result, and loud is the end of the scale that gives the clearest reading. Volume also carries feeling before words can, so a morning of noise she is allowed to make drains off what would come out later as a floor tantrum. Handing her the dial changes what the noise is for: she has to hold a number, watch other people follow it, and cut the sound off on eight. You get the loud out on purpose, at a time you chose, and the quiet numbers come easier all week.

days.safety: Close-range banging is loud enough to damage a 15-month-old's hearing. Keep Kreston a room's width from the buckets, work in short bursts with quiet gaps, and stop the moment he startles, covers his ears or turns away. Never let the spoons swing near his head.

days.title: High Notes, Low Notes
days.prepTonight: Wash eight jam jars or tumblers of the same size, stand them on a tray on the table, and fill a pitcher with water beside them.

schedule.label: Opening Activity
schedule.name: One Cup, Two Cups, Eight Cups

schedule.label: Get Outside
schedule.name: Leaves Still Up, Leaves Already Down

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: Up the Stairs, One Note at a Time

opening.title: One Cup, Two Cups, Eight Cups
opening.need: 8 jam jars on a tray · 1 pitcher of water · 1 small cup for pouring.
steps: Count the jars you washed last night along the tray on the table, left to right, and let her tell you which one she thinks will end up heaviest.
She pours eight cupfuls into jar one and seven into jar two, counting each pour out loud as it goes in. The row empties out as it goes along.
Stop there and leave the other six. Ask her what she thinks jar eight will look like when it only gets one, and tell her she fills the rest at 9:15.

main.title: Eight Jars and a Spoon
materials: 8 jam jars or glass tumblers, all the same size
Masking tape and 1 marker for the numbers
steps: Tape a strip in front of each jar and number them 1 to 8 in marker. She fills jars three to eight, counting the cupfuls down the row: six cups into jar three, five into jar four, on down to one cup into jar eight.
Top the pitcher up as she goes. Spills land on the tray.
One drop of food coloring in each jar if you have it. She stirs with the teaspoon and eight jars of water become eight different things.
Tap each jar on the rim with the teaspoon, working from one to eight, and let the line of sounds land before anyone says a word.
Ask which jar holds the most water and which made the deepest sound, then check her answer by tapping those two again.
She plays the whole ladder, one to eight and back down to one, counting as she taps.
main.tip: Say deep and thin rather than low and high for the first half hour.

outside.title: Leaves Still Up, Leaves Already Down
paras: Stand under one tree and count ten leaves still up in the branches, then ten already down at your feet. First week of October and most trees are half and half, so one tree gives you both. Point up on the counting up and crouch on the counting down.

days.infant: Kreston turns 16 months today. Say it out loud, because nobody else will. He stacks four blocks now and copies whatever a grown-up is doing, so hand him a leaf and hold your own up high.

second.title: Up the Stairs, One Note at a Time
second.intro: The jars gave her a ladder she could hear. The stairs give her one she can climb.
materials: The stairs, or a chair, the sofa and the floor as three heights
Masking tape and 1 marker for numbering the steps
The jars from this morning, left on their tray on the table as the reference
steps: Tape a numbered strip on the first eight stairs, 1 at the bottom. Shut the stair gate at the bottom with Kreston on the far side of it, and keep to one person on the stairs at a time.
She sits on stair one and sings a low note. Up to stair two, and her voice goes up with her. Follow her rather than lead.
Climb to eight, a note a stair, then come back down and let the voice drop with each step.
Leave the jars on the table and go back to them between climbs. Tap jar one with the teaspoon, then jar eight, and ask her which stair each one belongs on. The full deep one lives at the bottom.
Call a number. She climbs to that stair and sings the note she thinks lives there.
Swap. She calls the number, you climb, and you go to the wrong stair once so she can send you back.
Take the tape off the stairs before dinner. Tape underfoot on a staircase is a fall waiting to happen.
second.tip: The floor, the sofa and a chair make three heights if the stairs are out.

alternatives: Four jars instead of eight, and a lot more tapping.
Sing the numbers up and down without the stairs at all.
Pour the jars back into the pitcher, counting the cupfuls out.
Tap the jars while she hides her eyes and guesses high or low.
outAgain: Swimming, and count the steps into the water
The library, if the pool is booked out for lessons
Indoor playground, counting the steps up to the slide
A short walk while the light lasts, which is going fast now
days.krestonPM: He comes to the pool at 16 months and copies everything you do in the water. Hold his hands and count three, two, one before every lift and dip. Twenty minutes and out. October cold arrives fast and he will not say so until he shivers.

insight.headline: High and low is a confusing pair of words.
paras: Azlyn already uses high and low for where a thing sits on a shelf. Asking her to hear a high note means bolting a second meaning onto a word she has settled, and three-year-olds sort this out by lining the two up rather than by being told they are different. Climbing a stair while her voice rises gives her height, number and pitch moving together in one action, and the match does the teaching. Reaching for the top of her range while standing on the top stair is worth more than any explanation. Children whose parents sing with them hear the difference between two notes better, without a single lesson.

days.safety: Glass jars and a hard floor, and stairs with a 16-month-old who climbs. The jars stay on the tray on the table, never on the floor and never at the top of the stairs. The stair gate stays shut and one person is on the stairs at a time. Swimming this afternoon. Both children stay within arm's reach in the water at all times, and no float or seat is a substitute for your hands.

days.title: Stop on Seven
days.prepTonight: Check Monday's number line is still taped down the hall, stick down any corners that have lifted, and put eleven blank cards and a marker on the table.

schedule.label: Second Main Event
schedule.name: The Tower That Stops Where She Says

schedule.label: Her Job
schedule.name: Counting the Peas Onto Kreston's Tray

opening.title: The Number That Means Freeze
opening.need: 11 blank cards · 1 thick marker · masking tape.
steps: Write 0 to 10 on the cards, one numeral each, and let her take over on the ones she knows. These are the number cards for the rest of the week.
Spread all eleven face up on the table and ask her to choose the one that means stop. She will pick a big one.
Tape her choice to the door at her eye height. That number is the rule now, and everyone in the house has to obey it at 9:15.

main.title: The Number on the Door
materials: The taped number line from Monday, still down the hall
1 wooden spoon and 1 pan, or music on your phone
steps: Read the card on the door out loud together. Say it back and forth until she can tell you what happens when the count reaches it.
Bang the pan with the spoon and count up from one, slow and even, while she runs the hall from 0 to 10 and back.
On her number she freezes. Keep banging past it. The count is the cue, so the noise carrying on is what makes the number do the work.
Praise the stop, not the running. Hold the freeze for a slow three before you start the next count.
New card every round. She takes one off the table and tapes it up herself, and low numbers come round fast.
Swap over. She counts and bangs, you run the hall, and you miss the stop once so she gets to call you out.
main.tip: Count slower than feels sensible. The gap between nine and ten is where she does the work of getting ready to stop, and a fast count takes that away.

outside.title: Stopping at Every Third Tree
paras: Walk the road counting trees or lampposts out loud, and stop dead at every third one. Both of you, hands in the air, until she says go. October has the sidewalk covered, so count the piles she can kick through on the way as well. Turn round at the fifteenth and count them back down to one.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies whatever the rest of you are doing, so he will throw his hands up a beat after Azlyn does and keep walking. That gap is real. Stopping on a signal comes later than copying the shape of it, and he is working on the shape.

second.title: The Tower That Stops Where She Says
second.intro: She sits down for this one, and the rule comes with her. Stopping a hand mid-air is harder than stopping two feet.
materials: Paper and crayons for her stop cards
4 blocks or small boxes for Kreston
steps: Line the ten cups up beside her and put Kreston's four blocks down at the far end of the rug. She picks a card and props it against the pile.
She stacks one cup at a time, counting each one, and stops dead on her number with the next cup already in her hand.
Hold it there. Count a slow three with the cup in the air, then let her carry on to ten.
Bring the counting jar down to the table for one round. She drops buttons into a cup one at a time and stops on her number, then tips them back and the jar goes up high again.
Paper and crayons out. She makes her own stop cards, a numeral and a picture on each, and they can be any numbers she likes.
She hands you a stop card and you do the stacking. She calls the freeze, and you keep going one cup past it so she has to stop you.
Last tower goes to ten with no stop at all, and she knocks it down.
second.tip: She will fly past her number on the first two goes. Stopping wins over accuracy today, so let a tower stop on eight when the card says seven and count the stop as the win.

alternatives: Stop on three instead, and stack five cups.
Post buttons into a slot in a lid and stop on the number.
Draw a tower with the right number of cups on it.
Build the tower and let Kreston flatten it.
outAgain: Indoor playground, the quiet session, and count the steps up to the top slide
The library, if the quiet session is full
The park while the light holds, counting laps of the path
The store for one thing, counted out at the register
Home and the hall number line, if nobody wants a coat on
days.krestonPM: Give him the four blocks on the floor beside her cups. At 16 months he stacks four and knocks them down himself, which is his whole version of this afternoon. Count his up out loud as he goes, one, two, three, four, and he will hand you the fourth one to place.

insight.headline: Freezing on cue is genuine impulse control.
paras: Stopping a body that is already running takes more from Azlyn than starting one. She has to hold the rule in mind, track the count while she moves and override what her legs are doing, which are the three parts of what researchers call executive function. Games with a stop signal are one of the few things shown to move it. Tying the stop to a number rather than to the music cutting out makes it harder, because she cannot wait for silence to tell her. She has to keep her own count. Three-year-olds who play games like this get better at the stopping, and it shows up at bath time.

days.safety: Kreston stays out of the hall and at the far end of the room from the pan whichever of you is running it, because a body at full speed in a corridor does not stop for a 16-month-old. Sit him where you can see him from the hall, or use the music on your phone instead of the banging. Buttons are the size that chokes a 16-month-old. The jar round happens at the table with Kreston out of reach, the buttons are counted back in before he is on the rug again, and the jar goes up high after. Use tins for the tower only if the rims are smooth.

days.title: Clap It Back
days.prepTonight: Cut six cards out of a cereal box and leave them on the table with the marker, the crayons, six clothespins and a length of string.

opening.title: Two Claps, Then Wait
opening.need: your hands · her hands · a floor to sit on.
steps: Sit facing each other and clap twice. Wait. She claps twice back, and neither of you says anything about what the game is.
Three claps, then four. Count them out loud as you go so the number arrives with the sound.
Four claps with a gap in the middle. She will send back four in a row and lose the gap.

main.title: Four Beats, Then Your Turn
materials: 1 saucepan and the buckets from Monday
The counting jar, for counting out the beats
steps: Sit on the floor with the pan and the buckets between you and a spoon each.
Play four even beats on the pan, counting them out loud. She plays four back. Do it until it bores her, which takes about six goes.
Take the counting out. Play four beats in silence and let her count them in her head before she answers.

Lay one button from the counting jar on the floor for each beat as you play it, and leave a space where a beat is missing. She reads the row and plays it. The jar goes back up high when this round ends.
Move the same four beats around: hands, knees, floor, pan, bucket. The pattern stays the same and the sound changes.
She leads now. She plays, you copy, and you get one wrong on purpose so she has to fix you.
main.tip: Keep patterns to four beats today. Five is where a three-year-old drops the last one and hands back three, looking at you as though you changed it.

outside.title: The Railings and the Stick
paras: Find a stretch of railings and run a stick along them, counting the clicks. Slow first, then fast enough that neither of you can keep up with the number. Wet October railings ring where dry ones clack, and the same stick on a wooden fence goes dull. Try both and let her tell you which one she likes.

days.infant: Kreston is 16 months and copies chores, so give him his own short stick and let him drag it along the low part of the railings. Say the numbers over his clicks. At 16 months he has ten words and picks up new ones attached to something he is doing.

second.title: Four Dots and a Gap
second.intro: A rhythm disappears the second it stops. This afternoon hers goes onto a card and stays there.
materials: 6 cards cut from a cereal box
The jars from Tuesday and the hall number line, still up
steps: She plays four beats. Draw them on a card in marker as she plays, a dot for a beat and a gap for a silence.
Hand her the card and ask her to play what is on it. Point at each dot as she hits it so her eye travels along the row.
Six cards, six patterns, three hers and three yours, with a gap at the front of one.
She colors the cards with crayons. Every dot she colors is one she has to look at.
Tie the string between the front legs of two dining chairs, down at her knee height, tight enough to hold the cards. She pegs them along it in the order she picks, a peg to a card.
Play the whole row left to right, spoons on the buckets, counting the dots on each card as you reach it.

Finish the week: tap Tuesday's jars from one to eight with the metal teaspoon, walk the hall number line from 0 to 10, then play the card row once more. Take the string down and put it away, then peel the number line up off the hall floor with her, 10 back down to 0.
second.tip: Read the cards left to right every time and move your finger as you go.

alternatives: Two cards instead of six, and a lot of playing them.
Clap the patterns with no cards at all.
Play the row while she marches the hall number line.
outAgain: The pharmacy and the park bench, and she counts the change into your hand
The bakery, counting rolls into the bag
The park, for the leaf pile and a long run about
Indoor playground if the rain has set in
days.krestonPM: Sit him on the bench between you at the park with the paper bag from the pharmacy. At 16 months he copies chores, so let him hand things over one at a time and thank him for each. He carries this morning's stick the whole way there and back.

insight.headline: Copying a rhythm is harder than it looks, and it's a working memory task.
paras: Azlyn has to hold four beats and their spacing in her head while she waits, then get her hands to reproduce something that has already stopped existing. The four beats have to survive the gap between your hand stopping and hers starting. Nothing is left in front of her to check against. That is auditory working memory, and it sits underneath following instructions, remembering a request from the hallway and later on sounding out a word. Children who copy a rhythm well at three tend to read more easily later. Leading it is harder again, because she has to invent a pattern and hold it steady while she watches you get it wrong.

days.safety: The card line runs low between two chair legs, pulled tight and never left slack or in a loop, so there is nothing at either child's neck height. Kreston stays off that stretch of floor the whole time it is up. Take it down and put it away the moment the cards come off, because a length of string at toddler height is a strangulation risk. Buttons go on the floor only while the two of you are sitting over them, and they are back in the jar and up high before Kreston is down.
